concepts.name: Establishment, legal nature and rationale of the NITI Aayog
concepts.description: How and why the NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015, its non-constitutional and non-statutory status, and the three foundations and the style of working that the Government set out for it.
concepts.idea: The NITI Aayog is a Cabinet-resolution think tank that replaced the Planning Commission to move from command and control to cooperative, bottom-up policy-making.
concepts.rule: On 13 August 2014 the Government scrapped the 65-year-old Planning Commission and announced a new body; the NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) was established on 1 January 2015 as its successor. Like the Planning Commission it was created by an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet, so it is neither constitutional nor statutory. It is the premier policy think tank of the Government and gives directional and policy inputs and technical advice to the Centre and States. The centre-to-state one-way flow of the Planning Commission era is to give way to a continuing partnership of States, with a collaborative and bottom-up approach in place of command and control. It rests on three foundations: States as equal partners (cooperative federalism), a knowledge hub, and a collaborative platform for implementation (pp.667-668).
concepts.example: A student asked whether the NITI Aayog is a statutory body answers that it is not, because it came from a Cabinet resolution of 1 January 2015 and not from an Act of Parliament.

concepts.name: Composition of the NITI Aayog
concepts.description: The Chairperson, Governing Council, Regional Councils, special invitees and the full-time organisational framework with its ranks and limits.
concepts.idea: The NITI Aayog pairs the Prime Minister as Chairperson with a Governing Council of Chief Ministers and a small full-time team whose ranks and numbers are fixed.
concepts.rule: The Prime Minister is the Chairperson. The Governing Council has the Chief Ministers of all States, the Chief Ministers of Union Territories with legislatures (Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir) and the Lt. Governors of the other Union Territories. Regional Councils are formed for a specified tenure on issues affecting more than one State or region, convened by the Prime Minister and chaired by the Chairperson or a nominee; special invitees are experts nominated by the Prime Minister. The full-time framework has a Vice-Chairperson (Cabinet Minister rank), full-time members (Minister of State rank), a maximum of two part-time members on rotation, a maximum of four ex-officio members from the Union Council of Ministers, a CEO appointed for a fixed tenure in the rank of Secretary, and a secretariat as deemed necessary (pp.668-669).
concepts.example: A Regional Council for the north-eastern States would have the Chief Ministers of the region and be chaired by the Chairperson or a nominee.

concepts.name: Cooperative and competitive federalism and the bodies attached to the NITI Aayog
concepts.description: Steps taken to foster cooperative federalism, the rankings and indices of competitive federalism, and the NILERD and the DMEO.
concepts.idea: The NITI Aayog works with States through meetings, models and rankings, and is supported by NILERD (autonomous) and the DMEO (attached office).
concepts.rule: The NITI Aayog brings States together as 'Team India' on the premise that strong States make a strong nation. Its cooperative-federalism steps include meetings with Chief Ministers, subgroups of Chief Ministers, sharing best practices, the Aspirational Districts Programme, model laws on land leasing and agriculture marketing, and models such as the DSSS and SATH (p.672). It promotes competitive federalism through transparent rankings and indices (School Education Quality, State Health, Composite Water Management, SDG, India Innovation) and monthly delta rankings of Aspirational Districts (pp.672-673). NILERD (formerly IAMR) is a central autonomous organisation, and the DMEO, set up in 2015 by merging the PEO (1952) and the IEO (2010), is an attached office whose 15 regional offices closed in 2017 (pp.673-674).
concepts.example: A State ranked low in the State Health Index receives hand-holding support from the NITI Aayog and is expected to improve in the next ranking.

concepts.name: The erstwhile Planning Commission: nature, functions, composition and criticism
concepts.description: The Planning Commission set up in 1950, its seven functions, how it was composed, and the criticism that it became a Super Cabinet.
concepts.idea: The Planning Commission was a non-statutory advisory staff agency that grew into a powerful directive body, criticised as a parallel cabinet.
concepts.rule: The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950 by an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet on the recommendation of the Advisory Planning Board (1946, K.C. Neogi), so it was neither constitutional nor statutory (p.674). Its seven functions covered assessing resources, formulating a plan, setting priorities, indicating retarding factors, deciding machinery, appraising progress and advising on referred matters; it was only a staff agency with no executive responsibility (p.674). It was chaired by the Prime Minister, with a Deputy Chairman as de facto executive head, part-time Central Ministers, four to seven full-time experts and a member-secretary; the States were not represented (p.675). Critics called it a Super Cabinet, Parallel Cabinet and Fifth Wheel of the Coach, the First ARC and K. Santhanam criticised its role, and P.V. Rajamannar noted an overlap with the Finance Commission (p.675).

concepts.name: The National Development Council and its link with the NITI Aayog
concepts.description: The NDC's origin, composition, objectives, functions, its last meeting and the reported transfer of its powers to the NITI Aayog's Governing Council.
concepts.idea: The NDC is a non-statutory forum of the Prime Minister, Union Cabinet Ministers and Chief Ministers that considered the Plan prepared by the Planning Commission.
concepts.rule: The National Development Council was established in August 1952 by an executive resolution on the recommendation of the First Five Year Plan (draft outline), and is neither constitutional nor statutory (p.675). It consists of the Prime Minister as chairman, all Union Cabinet Ministers (since 1967), the Chief Ministers of all States, the Chief Ministers or administrators of all Union Territories and the members of the Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog) (p.676). Its objectives are cooperation of States, mobilising national resources, common economic policies and balanced development; its functions include prescribing guidelines for the Plan, considering the Plan prepared by the Planning Commission, assessing resources and reviewing the Plan (p.676). Its last (57th) meeting on 27 December 2012 approved the 12th Plan, and on 1 January 2016 it was reported that its powers would pass to the NITI Aayog's Governing Council, though the chapter says no resolution had been passed (p.675).
